content.title: Volumes with Equilateral Triangle Cross Sections
content.overview: This lesson focuses on calculating the volume of a solid whose base is a region in the xy-plane and whose cross sections, taken perpendicular to an axis, are equilateral triangles. The method involves expressing the side length of the triangle as a function of the slicing variable, determining the area of a single cross section, and integrating that area over the specified interval.
learning_objectives: Identify the side length of a cross section based on the distance between two functions.
Apply the area formula for an equilateral triangle in terms of its side length.
Set up and evaluate a definite integral to find the total volume of a solid with known cross sections.
Assign correct cubic units to the resulting volume.

sections.title: Defining the Side Length
sections.content: To find the volume of a solid with known cross sections, first identify the base region in the xy-plane. If cross sections are perpendicular to the x-axis, the side length s(x) of each cross section is the vertical distance between the upper function f(x) and the lower function g(x). This is calculated as s(x) = f(x) - g(x). If the cross sections are perpendicular to the y-axis, the side length s(y) is the horizontal distance, calculated as right function minus left function.

sections.title: The Equilateral Triangle Area Formula
sections.content: The area A of an equilateral triangle with side length s is given by the formula A = (√3/4)s^2. In the context of volume by cross sections, the area becomes a function of the position along the axis of integration. For cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis, A(x) = (√3/4)[s(x)]^2. It is critical to include the constant (√3/4); omitting it is a frequent source of error.

sections.title: The Volume Integral
sections.content:
The volume V of the solid is the integral of the cross-sectional area function over the interval [a, b] that defines the base of the solid. The general formula is V = ∫[a, b] A(x) dx. Substituting the equilateral triangle area formula, we get V = ∫[a, b] (√3/4)[s(x)]^2 dx. Because (√3/4) is a constant, it can be moved outside the integral to simplify calculations: V = (√3/4) ∫[a, b] [s(x)]^2 dx.

![A linear sequence of steps: 1. Identify side length s(x). 2. Determine area formula A(x). 3. Set integral bounds. 4. Integrate A(x) over the interval.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/d285d18f-c97b-4d96-85a7-5d023e3df443-1786519388067-859.webp)

worked_examples.question: A solid has a base bounded by y = 0 and y = 1 + x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are equilateral triangles. Find the exact volume of the solid in cubic centimeters.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Identify the side length s(x). The top function is y = 1 + x and the bottom is y = 0. Thus, s(x) = (1 + x) - 0 = 1 + x.
Step 2: Set up the area function A(x). For equilateral triangles, A(x) = (√3/4)[s(x)]^2 = (√3/4)(1 + x)^2.
Step 3: Set up the integral with bounds x = 0 to x = 2. V = ∫[0, 2] (√3/4)(1 + x)^2 dx.
Step 4: Evaluate the integral. V = (√3/4) ∫[0, 2] (1 + 2x + x^2) dx = (√3/4) [x + x^2 + x^3/3] evaluated from 0 to 2.
Step 5: Plug in the bounds. At x = 2: (2 + 4 + 8/3) = 26/3. At x = 0: 0. 
Step 6: Final calculation. V = (√3/4)(26/3) = (13√3)/6 cubic centimeters.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the (√3/4) constant and treating the cross section as a square.
Squaring the entire integral instead of squaring the side length inside the integrand.
Using the wrong bounds (e.g., using y-limits for an x-axis integration).
Incorrectly identifying which function is the 'top' versus the 'bottom' in the base region.
exam_tips: Always sketch the base region to visualize the top and bottom functions clearly.
Pull the geometric constant (like √3/4) outside the integral immediately to avoid arithmetic errors during integration.
Check if the problem specifies the cross section is 'perpendicular to the x-axis' (integrate dx) or 'perpendicular to the y-axis' (integrate dy).
Ensure units are cubed (e.g., cm^3) since you are calculating volume.
content.recap: To find the volume of a solid with equilateral triangle cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis, determine the side length s(x) = top - bottom, square it, multiply by the constant √3/4, and integrate the resulting expression over the x-interval of the base.

knowledge_claims.content: The area of an equilateral triangle with side length s is A = (√3/4)s^2.
To find the side length s(x) for cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis, subtract the lower function g(x) from the upper function f(x).
The volume of a solid with known cross sections is the definite integral of the area function A(x) or A(y) over the interval of the base.
A common error is omitting the (√3/4) factor, which results in calculating the volume of a solid with square cross sections instead of equilateral triangles.
When cross sections are perpendicular to the x-axis, the limits of integration must be the x-coordinates of the boundaries of the base region.
The constant (√3/4) can be moved outside the integral sign to simplify the evaluation of the antiderivative.
The integrand in a volume problem represents the area of a single infinitesimal slice (cross section) of the solid.
Volume calculations must always result in units of cubic measure, such as cubic centimeters or units^3.
If a problem states cross sections are perpendicular to the y-axis, the side length must be expressed as a function of y, and the integration must be with respect to y.
The side length s(x) must be squared before multiplying by the geometric constant and integrating.
Unlike volumes of revolution which use pi (π), volumes with equilateral triangle cross sections use the square root of three (√3) in their area constant.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is used to evaluate the volume integral by finding the antiderivative and subtracting the value at the lower bound from the value at the upper bound.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Volumes with Cross Sections — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Volumes with Cross Sections: A solid with known cross-sectional area has volume equal to the integral of that area along the perpendicular axis.
options.B: Polar Area: Polar area over an angular interval is one half the integral of the squared radius, with intersections determining correct angular bounds.
options.C: Taylor and Maclaurin Series: Taylor coefficients are derivatives evaluated at the center divided by factorials, and Maclaurin series are centered at zero.
options.D: Differentiability and Continuity: Differentiability implies continuity, but corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities, and unequal one-sided derivatives can prevent differentiability.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because A solid with known cross-sectional area has volume equal to the integral of that area along the perpendicular axis. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Volumes with Cross Sections — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Sequence Limits: A sequence converges when its terms approach a finite value and diverges when no such limit exists.
options.B: Volumes with Cross Sections: A solid with known cross-sectional area has volume equal to the integral of that area along the perpendicular axis.
options.C: Power Series Intervals and Error: A power series has a radius and endpoint-dependent interval of convergence, while Taylor remainder bounds quantify approximation error.
options.D: Basic Derivative Rules: Constant, power, sum, product, and quotient rules determine derivatives efficiently while preserving the structure of the original function.
